docs.title: ETLRelay
docs.text:
ETLRelay is a lightweight Python framework for composing batch-oriented extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines.

Its core execution model is:

Source → Processor(s) → Sink

For file workflows, storage access and file-format handling are separate concerns. A file source composes a storage implementation with a reader; a file sink composes storage with a writer. This keeps the core pipeline independent of filesystem and serialization details.

docs.title: Current release scope
docs.text:
The 0.5.0 release extends ETLRelay's tested local CSV/Parquet pipeline model with SQL input and append-only SQL output through SQLAlchemy.

Current capabilities include:

  • An Arrow-backed Batch model and synchronous source → processor(s) → sink execution.
  • Local filesystem access through FileSystem and LocalFileSystem.
  • CSV and Parquet readers/writers composed through FileSource and FileSink.
  • Built-in column selection, column renaming, and row filtering processors.
  • SqlSource for parameterized SQL queries and SqlSink for append-only writes to existing SQL tables.
  • Unit, integration, round-trip, and functional tests for component behavior and composed local-file/SQLite pipelines.

SQLite is the repeatable SQL integration-test backend. Other SQLAlchemy dialects require their appropriate drivers and application-level verification; the project does not claim equal integration coverage for every database. SQL output tables must exist before a pipeline runs. SqlSink does not create or migrate tables, replace existing data, or retry failed operations.

S3, HDFS, and other remote filesystem/storage backends are outside the planned v1.0.0 scope. Additional storage and platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them; no particular backend or delivery date is promised.

ETLRelay remains pre-1.0 software. Its public APIs may evolve between minor releases.

docs.title: etlrelay.pipeline.pipeline.Pipeline
docs.text:
Coordinate batch processing between a source, processors, and a sink.

The pipeline obtains batches from a source, applies each configured processor in sequence, validates the resulting output schemas, and passes compatible batches to the sink.

The first processed output batch establishes the expected schema for the run. Subsequent output batches must have matching field names, field order, Arrow types, and nullability. Schema metadata differences are ignored. Zero-row batches participate in schema validation.

Processing is lazy and does not buffer all batches before writing. If a later batch has an incompatible schema, a ValueError is raised before that batch is yielded to the sink. Batches successfully written before a later failure are not rolled back.

Exceptions from the source, processors, or sink otherwise propagate to the caller.

docs.text:
Filter a batch using a single column comparison predicate.

Supported operators are ==, !=, <, <=, >, and >=. Comparisons use Apache Arrow compute operations without custom casting.

Rows whose comparison evaluates to false or null are excluded. The input schema is preserved, including when no rows match.

The processor can be reused across batches without retaining batch-specific state.

Example

from etlrelay.processors import FilterRows

processor = FilterRows(column="age", operator=">=", value=18) result = processor.process(batch)

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
ETLRelay composes batch-oriented ETL pipelines from a source, an ordered sequence of processors, and a sink.

Source → Processor(s) → Sink

A source produces batches, processors transform them, and a sink consumes the processed output. For file workflows, ETLRelay separates storage access from format-specific reading and writing.

docs.title: Batch
docs.text:
A Batch wraps a pyarrow.Table and provides the common tabular data representation used throughout ETLRelay.

The table retains its values and Arrow schema, including field names, field order, data types, and nullability. A processor may change the schema as part of a transformation; otherwise, the schema is preserved.

A batch containing zero rows is still a valid batch. Its schema remains available even when it contains no data rows.

docs.title: Source, Processor, and Sink
docs.text:
A Source implements read() and produces an iterable of batches.

A Processor implements:

process(batch: Batch) -> Batch

Processors operate on individual batches. The pipeline applies them in their configured order, passing each processor's output to the next processor. ETLRelay includes processors for selecting columns, renaming columns, and filtering rows. Applications can also provide implementations that satisfy the processor contract.

A Sink consumes an iterable of processed batches. A file sink composes a storage implementation with a writer to write batches to a configured destination.

docs.title: Storage and File Formats
docs.text:
Storage provides binary streams; readers and writers handle the file format.

FileSource → FileSystem → BinaryIO → Reader → Batch

Batch iterable → Writer → BinaryIO → FileSystem → Destination

FileSource composes a filesystem with a reader. FileSink composes a filesystem with a writer. This separates resource access from format-specific parsing and serialization.

The current implementation supports local filesystem access through LocalFileSystem, with CSV through CsvReader/CsvWriter and Parquet through ParquetReader/ParquetWriter. Select the reader and writer explicitly when constructing FileSource and FileSink; the file extension does not select a format automatically.

docs.title: CSV and Parquet Behavior
docs.text:
The file format is selected when composing the source or sink. FileSource and FileSink do not inspect the filename extension or choose a reader/writer automatically.

Behavior CSV Parquet Representation Text; no embedded Arrow schema Columnar binary format with schema and type information Reading types PyArrow infers types from text; exact schema round trips are not guaranteed Preserves schema and supported Arrow types represented in the Parquet file Multiple batches Serializes batches in order; a CSV stream has one header written by the first batch Serializes batches in order into one Parquet file Zero-row batch with schema Can write a header-only CSV Writes a valid schema-bearing zero-row Parquet file; the reader yields one empty batch with the schema Empty batch iterable Writes no bytes Raises WriterError because no schema is available to initialize the file Stream requirements Binary stream Reader: seekable binary stream; writer: writable binary stream supported by PyArrow

A zero-row batch and an empty batch iterable are different: the former still carries an Arrow schema; the latter carries no batch from which a schema can be obtained. ParquetWriter uses the first batch's schema and requires following batches to have the same schema. ETLRelay does not merge incompatible schemas or automatically cast batches.

Parquet preserves supported Arrow schema/type information and values for the types handled by the installed PyArrow version; this should not be read as a guarantee that every Arrow-specific type, extension type, or metadata field is losslessly represented by Parquet. The stream protocols use BinaryIO, which does not express seekability in its type signature. ParquetReader therefore has a stronger runtime requirement than the generic Reader protocol suggests. The caller/component that opens a stream retains responsibility for its lifecycle; readers and writers must not close caller-owned streams.

docs.title: Pipeline Execution
docs.text:
Pipeline coordinates the source, processors, and sink. Execution is synchronous, and batches are processed sequentially in source order.

The pipeline does not buffer all source batches before writing. Processed batches are yielded incrementally to the sink.

docs.title: Output Schema Compatibility
docs.text:
The first processed output batch establishes the expected schema for a pipeline run. Every subsequent processed output batch must have a compatible schema.

Compatibility requires matching:

  • Field names
  • Field order
  • Arrow field types
  • Field nullability

Schema metadata differences are ignored when checking compatibility.

Schema validation takes place after all configured processors have run. This allows processors to normalize inputs with different schemas into compatible output schemas.

If a processed batch has an incompatible schema, the pipeline raises ValueError before yielding that batch to the sink. The pipeline does not automatically merge schemas, cast values, or reconcile incompatible outputs.

Zero-row batches participate in schema validation just like non-empty batches.

docs.title: Empty Sources and Zero-Row Batches
docs.text:
An empty source iterable and a zero-row batch represent different conditions.

  • Zero-row batch: The source produces a Batch containing a zero-row Arrow table. The batch passes through the configured processors, participates in schema validation, and is delivered to the sink if processing succeeds.
  • Empty source iterable: The source produces no batches. No processors are called, and the sink is not invoked.

The presence of a batch, rather than its row count, determines whether the pipeline has data to process.

docs.title: Exceptions and Partial Writes
docs.text:
Exceptions raised while reading from a source, iterating over its batches, processing a batch, validating its output schema, or writing to a sink propagate to the caller. ETLRelay does not wrap these errors in a separate pipeline exception hierarchy.

If a later batch fails, batches successfully written before the failure are not automatically rolled back. The pipeline does not provide transactional execution across multiple batches.

docs.title: SQL Sources and Sinks
docs.text:
SqlSource and SqlSink are direct implementations of the Source and Sink contracts. They do not route database I/O through FileSystem, Reader, or Writer components.

SqlSource executes a SQLAlchemy text query. Supply values through the optional parameters mapping, using named bind markers such as :status. A non-empty result becomes one Arrow-backed Batch; an empty query result produces no batches. The current source materializes query results in memory, so it is not a streaming or paginated reader.

SqlSink appends rows to a destination table that must already exist. It reflects the table and validates batch column names before inserting. It does not create/replace a table, update or upsert rows, migrate a schema, or retry a failed operation. Destination columns omitted from a batch must be satisfied by defaults/nullability or database constraints will fail.

The SQLAlchemy Engine is created and owned by the caller. ETLRelay closes the query connection/result and the sink's per-batch transaction contexts; it does not dispose the engine. SQLite is the repeatable integration backend. Other SQLAlchemy dialects need their driver and application-level validation.

Transactions are per non-empty sink batch. A successful batch is committed independently; a later failure does not roll back earlier batches. Empty query results produce no batches, and SqlSink skips explicitly supplied zero-row batches.

Bound parameters apply to query values, not SQL identifiers or arbitrary SQL syntax. SqlSink delegates destination table identifier handling to SQLAlchemy's table reflection/insert APIs. Since SqlSource accepts caller-authored SQL text, callers must not interpolate untrusted input into it and must validate or allowlist any dynamic identifiers.

replace, ORM models, schema migrations, automatic retries, and a pipeline-wide transaction are not supported. See SQL source and sink architecture for the full contract.

docs.title: Current Scope
docs.text:
ETLRelay provides synchronous, batch-oriented pipeline execution with local CSV/Parquet I/O, SQL input/output, and a small set of built-in processors.

The local storage contract, including binary stream modes, path containment, error propagation, output creation, overwrite behavior, and stream cleanup, is documented in the local filesystem architecture.

S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends are outside the v0.4.0 milestone and planned v1.0.0 scope. Additional storage and platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them. No particular backend or delivery date is promised.

Scheduling, distributed execution, parallel processing, automatic retries, and automatic schema reconciliation are not provided by the current pipeline implementation. Additional capabilities should be introduced when concrete requirements justify them and their scope is established.

docs.title: Development

pyright

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This guide demonstrates a local CSV transformation pipeline and shows how to switch the same composition model to Parquet. Both formats use the same file source/sink, storage, and processor abstractions.

The example selects columns, renames a column, and filters rows before writing the results to a new CSV file.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or newer.
  • ETLRelay installed in your environment.
  • A local CSV input file.

Install ETLRelay from the package repository:

python -m pip install etlrelay

docs.title: Prepare the input file
docs.text:
Create a data directory and save the following as data/input.csv:

name,age,department
Alice,17,Engineering
Bob,25,Data
Charlie,18,QA
Diana,16,Data
Evan,42,Engineering

The pipeline will write its output to data/output.csv.

docs.title: Build and run a pipeline
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

from etlrelay.pipeline import Pipeline
from etlrelay.processors import FilterRows, RenameColumns, SelectColumns
from etlrelay.readers import CsvReader
from etlrelay.security import PathValidator
from etlrelay.sinks import FileSink
from etlrelay.sources import FileSource
from etlrelay.storage import LocalFileSystem
from etlrelay.writers import CsvWriter


data_dir = Path("data").resolve()

storage = LocalFileSystem(
    path_validator=PathValidator(base_path=data_dir),
)

source = FileSource(
    path="input.csv",
    storage=storage,
    reader=CsvReader(),
)

sink = FileSink(
    path="output.csv",
    storage=storage,
    writer=CsvWriter(),
)

pipeline = Pipeline(
    source=source,
    processors=[
        SelectColumns(columns=["name", "age"]),
        RenameColumns(mapping={"name": "customer_name"}),
        FilterRows(column="age", operator=">=", value=18),
    ],
    sink=sink,
)

pipeline.run()

Run the script from the directory containing data/. The directory and input file must already exist.

docs.title: Understand the transformations
docs.text:
The processors execute in their configured order:

  1. SelectColumns retains name and age, dropping department.
  2. RenameColumns changes name to customer_name.
  3. FilterRows retains rows where age >= 18.

Each processor receives the previous processor's output. The pipeline then passes the processed batches to the CSV writer and sink.

docs.title: Expected output
docs.text:
After running the pipeline, data/output.csv contains:

"customer_name","age"
"Bob",25
"Charlie",18
"Evan",42

The output preserves the order of the matching input rows and contains only the selected and renamed columns.

For more details on batch behavior, empty inputs, and output schema compatibility, see Core Concepts. For constructor parameters and validation behavior, see the API Reference.

docs.title: Using Parquet
docs.text:
The same composition model supports Parquet. Select the format explicitly by supplying ParquetReader() to FileSource and ParquetWriter() to FileSink; ETLRelay does not infer the format from a filename extension. The executable example at examples/parquet_pipeline.py creates a small input file, applies the same select/rename/filter processors as the CSV example, and writes data/output.parquet.

The central composition looks like this:

from etlrelay.readers import ParquetReader
from etlrelay.sources import FileSource
from etlrelay.sinks import FileSink
from etlrelay.writers import ParquetWriter

source = FileSource(
    path="input.parquet",
    storage=storage,
    reader=ParquetReader(),
)
sink = FileSink(
    path="output.parquet",
    storage=storage,
    writer=ParquetWriter(),
)

Parquet retains its supported schema and data types, while CSV is text-based and infers types when read. A ParquetWriter requires at least one batch to establish its schema: an empty iterable raises WriterError. A zero-row Batch with a schema is valid and creates a schema-bearing Parquet file. ParquetReader requires a seekable binary stream; the reader/writer contracts are stream-based and leave stream lifecycle management to the component that opened the stream. See Reader and Writer and Core Concepts for format-specific behavior and limitations.

docs.title: Using SQL with SQLite
docs.text:
The following small example creates an in-memory SQLite database, reads selected orders with a bound query parameter, removes an unused column, and appends the processed rows to an existing table. It requires SQLAlchemy and the project's declared dependencies; it uses no credentials or external database service.

The complete runnable version is examples/sqlite_pipeline.py.

from sqlalchemy import Column, Float, Integer, MetaData, String, Table, create_engine

from etlrelay.pipeline import Pipeline
from etlrelay.processors import SelectColumns
from etlrelay.sinks import SqlSink
from etlrelay.sources import SqlSource

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")  # in-memory SQLite; no credentials
metadata = MetaData()

orders = Table(
    "orders", metadata,
    Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),
    Column("customer", String, nullable=False),
    Column("status", String, nullable=False),
    Column("total", Float, nullable=False),
)
Table(
    "processed_orders", metadata,
    Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),
    Column("customer", String, nullable=False),
    Column("total", Float, nullable=False),
)
metadata.create_all(engine)  # setup for this demo; SqlSink does not create tables

with engine.begin() as connection:
    connection.execute(orders.insert(), [
        {"id": 1, "customer": "Avery", "status": "ready", "total": 18.5},
        {"id": 2, "customer": "Riley", "status": "held", "total": 27.0},
    ])

pipeline = Pipeline(
    source=SqlSource(
        engine,
        "SELECT id, customer, status, total FROM orders WHERE status = :status",
        parameters={"status": "ready"},
    ),
    processors=[SelectColumns(columns=["id", "customer", "total"])],
    sink=SqlSink(engine, "processed_orders"),
)
pipeline.run()

# The engine belongs to the application. Dispose it when all DB work is done.
engine.dispose()

Important contract details:

  • SqlSource binds query values with parameters; do not interpolate untrusted values into SQL text. Bind parameters cannot stand in for table/column identifiers.
  • SqlSink is append-only and requires the destination table to exist with compatible columns. It does not implement replace, ORM models, or schema migrations.
  • Each non-empty batch is committed in its own transaction. Earlier batches remain committed if a later batch fails.
  • The application owns the SQLAlchemy engine. ETLRelay closes connections/results it opens but does not dispose the engine.
  • SQLite is the continuously tested reference backend; other SQLAlchemy dialects need the matching driver and independent verification.

See SQL source and sink architecture and the API Reference for full behavior and limitations.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This roadmap defines incremental, testable milestones from the current local-file pipeline implementation to a stable ETLRelay 1.0.0 release.

The target for 1.0.0 is a lightweight, synchronous, batch-oriented ETL framework that can read from local files or SQL, apply a small set of transformations, and write to local files or SQL. File storage and serialization remain separate concerns. YAML configuration and a small CLI make pipelines usable without writing Python for every job.

The roadmap is feature-led, not date-led. A version should be released when its acceptance criteria are met; the version numbers are proposed milestones, not a promise to publish every milestone on a fixed schedule.

docs.title: Current project status
docs.text:
Status Version Milestone Released 0.1.0 Experimental local CSV pipeline Released 0.1.x Stabilization and compatible fixes Released 0.2.0 Batch contract and built-in processors Released 0.3.0 Parquet format support Released 0.4.0 Storage contract stabilization Released 0.5.0 SQL source and sink Planned 0.6.0 onward YAML configuration, CLI, and v1.0 readiness milestones

The latest released milestone is 0.5.0. Releases 0.4.0 and 0.5.0 stabilized local filesystem behavior and added SQL source/sink support. The next planned milestone is 0.6.0, declarative YAML configuration. Later milestones describe intended scope and may be revised as implementation and testing clarify dependencies.

docs.title: Versioning policy
docs.text:
ETLRelay is in initial development, so 0.y.z is appropriate while the public API is still evolving. Semantic Versioning explicitly says that a 0.y.z public API should not yet be considered stable and recommends 0.1.0 as a reasonable starting point. See Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 and the Python Packaging User Guide's versioning discussion.

Until 1.0.0:

  • Use a patch release such as 0.1.1 for compatible fixes to a published release.
  • Use a minor release such as 0.2.0 for a coherent feature milestone. Public APIs may still evolve before 1.0.0, but document notable breaking changes.
  • Never replace or modify an already-published release. Publish a new version instead.
  • Use a release candidate such as 1.0.0rc1 only when the intended 1.0.0 feature set is complete and the remaining work is validation and defect correction.

docs.title: 0.1.0 — Experimental local CSV pipeline (released)
docs.text:
Outcome: Published the initial experimental local CSV pipeline. This release established the initial file-to-file execution path; it did not promise API stability.

The original release scope covered:

  • Batch backed by an Apache Arrow table.
  • Source, Processor, and Sink protocols.
  • Synchronous Pipeline orchestration.
  • PathValidator for local path containment.
  • FileSystem protocol and LocalFileSystem implementation.
  • Stream-based Reader and Writer protocols.
  • CsvReader and CsvWriter.
  • FileSource and FileSink composed from storage and format components.
  • Unit, integration, and functional tests for the local CSV path.
  • Architecture and usage documentation that matches the actual implementation.

The original release checks are preserved below as historical reference, not as open tasks for the current milestone.

Original release checks:

  • Full test suite, Ruff lint/format, and configured Pyright checks.
  • Successful source distribution and wheel builds.
  • Clean-environment installation and import/usage smoke test.
  • Accurate README instructions and example.
  • Correct project metadata, licence, package contents, and supported Python version.
  • Release notes describing pre-1.0.0 API evolution.
  • Git tag and retained release artifacts.

For future releases, uv build is the recommended package-build check. The Python Packaging User Guide describes building source and wheel distributions and supports using TestPyPI to rehearse publication: Building and Publishing.

docs.title: 0.1.x — Stabilize the first release (released patch line)
docs.text:
Goal: Correct defects found during initial use without expanding the feature set unnecessarily.

Scope:

  • Fix defects in the pipeline, batch, path validation, local storage, CSV reading, or CSV writing.
  • Improve error messages where they currently obscure the failing operation.
  • Correct packaging, installation, documentation, and typing issues.

Do not use patch releases to sneak in unrelated, large features.

docs.title: 0.2.0 — Batch contract and built-in processors (released)
docs.text:
Goal: Make ETLRelay useful for more than an untransformed file copy.

Scope:

  • Document and test Batch semantics, including schemas, types, zero-row tables, and empty iterables.
  • Define what happens when batches in one output stream have incompatible schemas.
  • Add a small set of processors, prioritizing:
  • SelectColumns;
  • RenameColumns;
  • FilterRows with a deliberately limited and documented predicate model.
  • Verify processor ordering and behavior across multiple batches.
  • Keep the processor interface as process(batch) -> Batch.

Done when: A tested local CSV pipeline can select, rename, and filter columns/rows while preserving documented schema and empty-batch behavior.

Not in scope: A general-purpose expression language, user-supplied code evaluation, or a large processor catalogue.

docs.title: 0.3.0 — Parquet format support (released)
docs.text:
Goal: Support a second high-value tabular format while retaining the format/storage boundary.

Scope:

  • Implement ParquetReader and ParquetWriter against the existing stream-based reader/writer protocols where the chosen Arrow APIs support that contract.
  • Test schema and type preservation, empty data, malformed input, and round trips.
  • Verify that the same reader/writer components work with LocalFileSystem without special cases in FileSource or FileSink.
  • Document CSV and Parquet behavior, including limitations and format-specific differences.

Done when: Local CSV and Parquet sources/sinks work through the same file composition model.

docs.title: 0.4.0 — Storage contract stabilization (released)
docs.text:
Outcome: Stabilized and documented the FileSystem/LocalFileSystem contract used by the local-file pipelines. The release specifies stream ownership and cleanup, read/write behavior, missing-path handling, path containment, overwrite behavior, and error propagation.

The release retained local filesystem support only. S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends remain outside both the v0.4.0 milestone and the planned v1.0.0 scope. Additional storage/platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them; none is promised by this roadmap.

Done when: The contract is explicit and tested, LocalFileSystem satisfies it, and existing CSV/Parquet pipelines remain functional.

docs.title: 0.5.0 — SQL source and sink (released)
docs.text:
Outcome: Added SQLAlchemy-backed SqlSource and SqlSink as direct implementations of the core source/sink contracts, independent of file storage and reader/writer abstractions.

The release supports bound query-value parameters, conversion of query results to Arrow-backed batches, and append-only insertion into existing destination tables. SQLite provides repeatable integration coverage for reads, writes, SQL round trips, and mixed file/SQL functional pipelines.

The caller owns the SQLAlchemy engine. SqlSource closes query results/connections after reading; SqlSink opens one transaction per non-empty batch. Consequently, earlier batches remain committed if a later batch fails. An empty SQL query returns no batches. The sink skips zero-row batches and requires the destination table to exist with compatible columns.

The SQL API does not implement replace, ORM-model integration, table creation/schema migrations, automatic retries, or pipeline-wide transactions. SQLite is the reference integration backend; support for other SQLAlchemy dialects requires the relevant driver and verification.

Done when: SQL input and append-only output compose with ETLRelay pipelines, value parameters are bound, and the behavior and limitations are documented and tested.

docs.title: 0.6.0 — Declarative YAML configuration
docs.text:
Goal: Let users define supported pipelines without writing Python assembly code.

Scope:

  • Define and document a versioned YAML schema for source, processor sequence, and sink.
  • Validate required properties and types before execution.
  • Resolve only explicitly supported component types through a small, explicit mapping.
  • Support configured storage and file formats where implemented.
  • Reference secrets through environment variables or another clearly documented mechanism; do not accept plaintext secrets as the recommended approach.
  • Reject unknown component types, unknown properties where appropriate, invalid combinations, and malformed configuration with actionable errors.
  • Do not use eval, arbitrary imports, or unrestricted Python execution to construct pipelines.

Done when: YAML configuration builds the same pipeline as direct Python composition and invalid configuration is rejected before the pipeline starts.

docs.title: 0.7.0 — Command-line interface
docs.text:
Goal: Make the framework practical to run from a shell or automation script.

Initial commands:

  • etlrelay run pipeline.yaml
  • etlrelay validate pipeline.yaml
  • etlrelay version

Scope:

  • Define useful process exit codes.
  • Print actionable validation and execution errors.
  • Keep secrets and sensitive payloads out of terminal output.
  • Keep the CLI thin; pipeline construction and execution logic belong in the underlying library.
  • Test commands without requiring external databases or cloud resources for the unit suite.

Done when: A user can validate and run a supported YAML pipeline through the installed CLI.

docs.title: 0.8.0 — Security, errors, and operational readiness
docs.text:
Goal: Close cross-cutting gaps before the API is frozen.

Scope:

  • Review path containment and local storage behavior, including symlinks and output destinations.
  • Review SQL parameterization and identifier validation.
  • Validate configuration before side effects occur.
  • Establish a small, consistent exception/error-reporting policy without wrapping every error in a generic framework exception.
  • Add useful standard-library logging at component boundaries where needed.
  • Redact connection secrets, credentials, and sensitive values from errors/logging.
  • Document resource/stream ownership, overwrite behavior, empty-batch behavior, and failure propagation.
  • Add dependency and package checks to CI.
  • Verify the package can be installed and used from its built artifacts, not only from the repository checkout.

Done when: Security-relevant behavior is tested at the layer responsible for the risk, and failures are diagnosable without leaking secrets.

docs.title: 0.9.0 — Feature-complete beta and API review
docs.text:
Goal: Validate the intended v1.0 feature set and stop adding new features.

Scope:

  • Feature freeze.
  • Review public names, constructors, protocol signatures, configuration schema, CLI behavior, and documented exceptions.
  • Test full pipelines across supported combinations: local CSV, local Parquet, and SQL input/output.
  • Test empty inputs, empty batches, schema mismatches, malformed data, inaccessible resources, processor failures, sink failures, and stream cleanup.
  • Test a clean install on each supported Python version/platform combination the project claims to support.
  • Complete README, quick start, examples, API reference, configuration reference, security notes, contribution instructions, and release notes.
  • Document unsupported features and known limitations.

Done when: No required v1.0 feature remains unimplemented, release-blocking defects are resolved, and the project can maintain a clear public API contract.

docs.title: 1.0.0rc1 — Release candidate
docs.text: Cut a release candidate only after 0.9.0 has passed the feature-complete criteria. Use release candidates for final packaging validation, integration feedback, and defect correction—not new features. Publish another candidate if fixes materially affect the release, then proceed to 1.0.0 when the release criteria remain satisfied.

docs.title: 1.0.0 — Stable initial release
docs.text:
ETLRelay 1.0.0 is ready when a user can:

  1. Install the package using documented instructions.
  2. Define a supported pipeline in YAML.
  3. Read data from the local filesystem or a supported SQL source.
  4. Apply the documented set of built-in transformations.
  5. Write to a local file or supported SQL sink.
  6. Run the pipeline through the CLI.
  7. Diagnose failures using documented errors and logs.

The stable API, supported Python versions, supported input/output formats, configuration schema, CLI contract, and compatibility policy must be documented. Breaking changes to the public API after 1.0.0 should follow the project's published versioning policy.

docs.title: Potential post-1.0 expansions (not commitments)
docs.text:
The initial stable release intentionally focuses on config-driven execution of pipelines using local files and SQL. Additional integrations and capabilities may be considered after 1.0.0, based on use cases, maintenance cost, compatibility with the existing architecture, and available development effort.

Potential areas for future review include, but are not limited to:

  • Remote and distributed storage, including S3 and HDFS.
  • Additional database, data-warehouse, and analytical-platform integrations, potentially including Snowflake and Hive.
  • Excel and other file formats.
  • Generic API source/sink implementations.
  • Scheduling, retries, distributed processing, concurrency, and orchestration services.
  • Web UI, job queue, monitoring server, and data catalog/lineage systems.
  • Expanded custom-component loading or plugin mechanisms.
  • Larger processor libraries or a general-purpose expression language.

These examples describe areas that may be evaluated, not features promised for a particular release. After v1.0.0, review candidate enhancements as a separate roadmap decision: identify concrete use cases, define acceptance criteria, estimate implementation and maintenance costs, and determine priority and sequencing. Do not assume that every listed integration will be implemented.

docs.title: Release hygiene
docs.text:
Before every public release:

  • Run the full test, lint, format, and type-check suites.
  • Build the wheel and source distribution.
  • Install and smoke-test the built package in a clean environment.
  • Review the changelog and release notes.
  • Ensure the version in package metadata matches the Git tag.
  • Test publication through TestPyPI when useful, then publish the actual release artifact.

The etlrelay distribution has already been published to PyPI; see the ETLRelay project page. Before each release, verify that package metadata, the built wheel and source distribution, the Git tag, and the release notes all identify the intended version. Revisit distribution-name availability only if the project proposes changing its published package name.

docs.text:
Version Status Milestone Release outcome 0.1.0 Released Experimental local CSV pipeline Initial local CSV pipeline published 0.1.x Released Stabilization Compatible fixes and documentation improvements 0.2.0 Released Batch contract and processors Basic useful transformations 0.3.0 Released Parquet CSV and Parquet through shared reader/writer interfaces 0.4.0 Released Storage contract stabilization Documented and tested local filesystem behavior; no remote-storage implementation 0.5.0 Released SQL source/sink Tested SQLite reads/writes and mixed file/SQL pipelines 0.6.0 Planned YAML Validated declarative pipelines 0.7.0 Planned CLI Validate and run pipelines from a shell 0.8.0 Planned Security and operational readiness Security review, errors/logging, installation and CI gates 0.9.0 Planned Feature-complete beta Feature freeze and full API review 1.0.0rc1 Planned Release candidate Final validation and feedback 1.0.0 Planned Stable release Documented, usable, tested config-driven ETL product

docs.title: Security
docs.text: ETLRelay is experimental pre-1.0 software. It should be evaluated in a non-production environment before it is used for important or sensitive workloads.

docs.title: Local filesystem paths
docs.text:
PathValidator resolves candidate paths and verifies that their resolved locations remain within the configured base directory. It checks path containment; it deliberately does not check existence. The filesystem operation determines whether a read or write succeeds.

This validation is not an operating-system sandbox and does not eliminate time-of-check/time-of-use races if another process can change the filesystem concurrently. Run ETLRelay with only the filesystem permissions it needs and use a dedicated working directory where appropriate.

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text: ETLRelay does not provide a complete filesystem sandbox, credentials vault, SQL authorization/query-policy layer, external API security model, or remote-storage security model. SQL query values can be bound through SqlSource, and SqlSink delegates destination-table statement construction to SQLAlchemy; these mechanisms do not make caller-authored SQL text or uncontrolled identifiers safe. The application remains responsible for query structure, database permissions, and secret handling.

docs.title: SQL values and identifiers
docs.text:
SqlSource supports SQLAlchemy bound parameters for query values. Use named placeholders (for example, :customer_id) and pass the value separately through parameters; do not interpolate untrusted values into SQL text. This is a narrow parameterization facility, not a complete SQL authorization or query-policy layer.

SQL identifiers such as table and column names cannot be supplied as ordinary bind parameters. SqlSink passes the configured destination table and optional schema to SQLAlchemy table-reflection/insert APIs, which handle dialect-aware identifier quoting. If an application constructs dynamic source query text, it must keep the query structure trusted and validate/allowlist dynamic identifiers. Never treat caller-controlled SQL text as safe merely because query values are bound.

The application is responsible for creating a least-privilege database engine/connection, protecting any credentials in real connection URLs, and following its database's authorization rules. Documentation examples use in-memory SQLite and contain no credentials.

The file-storage implementation supports the local filesystem only. S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends remain outside the planned v1.0.0 scope. SQL sources and sinks are separate SQLAlchemy-backed components; SQLite is the repeatable integration-test backend, while other database dialects need their matching driver and independent verification.

Additional storage or platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them. No particular integration or release date is promised.

For reporting suspected vulnerabilities, follow the procedure in the repository's Security policy.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FileSink is a sink component responsible for writing ETLRelay batches to a configured file resource.

It composes two independent components:

  • FileSystem, which provides a writable binary stream for the destination.
  • Writer, which serializes an iterable of Batch objects into the supplied stream.

FileSink does not depend on a particular storage implementation or file format. This allows it to work with LocalFileSystem and future storage implementations, as well as CsvWriter and future writers, without changing its implementation.

docs.text:

    class FileSystem {

    }

    }

    FileSystem <|.. LocalFileSystem
    Writer <|.. CsvWriter

    FileSink --> FileSystem : uses
    FileSink --> Writer : uses

    LocalFileSystem --> PathValidator : validates paths with

    Writer --> Batch : consumes

docs.title: FileSink
docs.text:
FileSink is responsible for:

  • Storing the configured destination path.
  • Opening the destination through the supplied FileSystem.
  • Passing the iterable of batches and writable stream to the supplied Writer.
  • Opening the destination once per write operation rather than once per batch.
  • Ensuring the stream is closed after writing, including when serialization fails.
  • Implementing the Sink protocol.

FileSink is not responsible for:

  • Implementing filesystem operations.
  • Validating local filesystem path containment.
  • Serializing CSV or other file formats.
  • Transforming or constructing Batch objects.
  • Selecting a storage backend or writer implementation.
  • Orchestrating pipeline execution.
  • Defining format-specific behavior for empty batches.
  • Implementing application-level logging.

docs.title: FileSystem
docs.text:
FileSystem defines the storage contract used to open the destination for writing.

Its implementations handle storage-specific behavior, including resource access, opening writable streams, and any applicable path validation.

FileSink depends on the protocol rather than directly on LocalFileSystem.

docs.title: Writer
docs.text:
Writer defines the contract for serializing an iterable of Batch objects into a binary stream.

Its implementations handle format-specific serialization. For example, CsvWriter serializes batches into CSV data using PyArrow.

The writer is responsible for processing the iterable according to its contract, including handling empty batches and determining how multiple batches are represented in one output resource.

FileSink does not need to know how the writer serializes the batches.

docs.title: Dependency Relationship
docs.text:
Sink
 ▲
 │ implements
 │
FileSink
 ├── FileSystem
 │      └── LocalFileSystem
 │              └── PathValidator
 │
 └── Writer
        └── CsvWriter

FileSink depends on the FileSystem and Writer protocols, not their concrete implementations.

This enables different combinations without modifying FileSink:

LocalFileSystem + CsvWriter
LocalFileSystem + ParquetWriter
S3Storage       + CsvWriter
HdfsStorage     + CsvWriter

Additional combinations can be supported as new storage and writer implementations are introduced.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The sink coordinates the following operations:

FileSink.write(batches)
          │
          ▼
FileSystem.open_write(path)
          │
          ▼
    BinaryIO stream
          │
          ▼
Writer.write(batches, stream)
          │
          ▼
   Serialized file data
          │
          ▼
       filesystem

The storage implementation provides the writable stream. The writer serializes the iterable of batches into that stream.

The stream is managed using a context manager so that it is closed after writing, including when serialization raises an exception.

A single call to FileSink.write() represents one output operation for the configured destination. All batches supplied in that call are handled by the writer through the same stream.

The sink does not buffer the entire iterable or independently iterate over it before passing it to the writer.

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Operation Expected behavior Construct with path, storage, and writer Stores the supplied dependencies and destination path Write an iterable of batches Delegates serialization to the supplied writer Write multiple batches Passes all batches through a single output stream Write an empty iterable Delegates empty-input handling to the writer Write an iterable containing empty batches Delegates empty-batch handling to the writer Write to a new valid local destination Creates the destination file when the parent directory exists and access is permitted Write to an invalid local path Propagates the path-validation error from local storage Write when storage access fails Propagates the underlying storage error Write when serialization fails Propagates the writer's exception Complete or fail a write Closes the opened stream Supply another storage implementation Works without modifying FileSink, provided it satisfies FileSystem Supply another writer implementation Works without modifying FileSink, provided it satisfies Writer

Exceptions are propagated rather than wrapped in a new FileSink exception hierarchy.

For the current local filesystem implementation, opening a destination for writing uses binary write mode. An existing destination is therefore truncated, while a new destination is created if its parent directory exists and filesystem access is permitted. Parent directories are not created automatically.

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
FileSink has one primary responsibility: coordinating storage access and serialization to deliver batches to a file resource.

It does not implement filesystem operations or format-specific serialization.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
New storage backends and writer implementations can be introduced without modifying FileSink.

For example, adding ParquetWriter or S3Storage does not require changes to the sink implementation.

No factory, registry, or plugin framework is required at this stage.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text:
Any implementation satisfying FileSystem can replace another storage implementation, and any implementation satisfying Writer can replace another writer.

Substitutions must preserve their respective contracts, including writable-stream behavior, iterable consumption, and exception propagation.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text:
FileSink depends on two small protocols:

  • FileSystem provides writable resource access.
  • Writer provides format-specific serialization.

Neither protocol needs unrelated operations such as pipeline orchestration or data transformation.

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
FileSink depends on protocols rather than concrete storage and writer classes.

This keeps sink orchestration independent of local filesystem details and particular file formats.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The initial implementation should remain small:

  • Accept a destination path, FileSystem, and Writer.
  • Use FileSystem.open_write() to obtain the output stream.
  • Pass the iterable of batches and stream to Writer.write().
  • Open the destination once per write operation.
  • Close the stream reliably.
  • Propagate underlying exceptions.
  • Avoid format detection, factories, registries, retries, and append-mode configuration until concrete requirements justify them.

The central design principle is:

FileSink coordinates serialization and storage; the writer handles the format and iterable of batches, while the storage implementation handles the destination.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FileSource is a source component responsible for reading data from a configured file resource and producing ETLRelay Batch objects.

It composes two independent components:

  • FileSystem, which provides access to the resource through a binary stream.
  • Reader, which parses the resource and produces an iterable of Batch objects.

FileSource does not depend on a particular storage implementation or file format. This allows it to work with LocalFileSystem and future storage implementations, as well as CsvReader and future readers, without changing its implementation.

docs.title: FileSource
docs.text:
FileSource is responsible for:

  • Storing the configured resource path.
  • Opening the resource through the supplied FileSystem.
  • Passing the resulting binary stream to the supplied Reader.
  • Exposing the reader's batches through the Source interface.
  • Ensuring the opened stream remains available while batches are being read.
  • Closing the stream when iteration finishes, fails, or is explicitly closed.

FileSource is not responsible for:

  • Implementing filesystem operations.
  • Validating local filesystem path containment.
  • Parsing CSV or other file formats.
  • Constructing Batch objects directly.
  • Transforming data.
  • Writing files.
  • Orchestrating pipeline execution.

docs.title: FileSystem
docs.text:
FileSystem defines the contract for accessing file resources.

Its implementations open resources for reading and provide binary streams. Storage-specific behavior, such as local path validation, remains within the concrete storage implementation.

FileSource depends on the protocol rather than on LocalFileSystem.

docs.title: Reader
docs.text:
Reader defines the contract for parsing a binary stream and producing an iterable of ETLRelay Batch objects.

Its implementations handle format-specific parsing. For example, CsvReader uses PyArrow to parse CSV data.

A reader may produce one or more batches. FileSource does not need to know how the reader divides its output into batches or how it interprets the underlying format.

This enables different combinations without modifying FileSource:

LocalFileSystem + CsvReader
LocalFileSystem + ParquetReader
S3Storage       + CsvReader
HdfsStorage     + CsvReader

Additional combinations can be supported as new storage and reader implementations are introduced.

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
The source coordinates the following operations:

FileSource.read()
       │
       ▼
FileSystem.open_read(path)
       │
       ▼
  BinaryIO stream
       │
       ▼
Reader.read(stream)
       │
       ▼
Iterable[Batch]
       │
       ▼
Pipeline

The reader determines how many batches are produced. FileSource exposes those batches through the Source interface without performing additional format conversion or transformation.

The stream must remain open while the reader's iterable is consumed. This is particularly important when a reader produces batches lazily. The stream should be managed with a context manager so that it is closed reliably when iteration completes or terminates with an exception.

The central design principle is:

FileSource coordinates resource access and batch production; the storage implementation handles the resource, and the reader handles the format.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FilterRows is a built-in implementation of the Processor contract. It filters a Batch using one comparison between a named column and a configured value. Comparisons and row filtering use Apache Arrow compute operations.

The processor provides a deliberately small predicate interface; it does not implement an expression language or custom casting system.

docs.title: Responsibilities and behavior
docs.text:
FilterRows stores one column name, one supported comparison operator, and one comparison value. It returns a new Batch containing rows that satisfy the predicate.

Supported operators are ==, !=, <, <=, >, and >=.

Scenario Behavior Unsupported operator Raises ValueError during initialization. Unknown or ambiguous column Raises ValueError when processing a batch. Incompatible comparison types Raises TypeError; no custom casting is performed. Comparison evaluates to null Excludes the row. No rows match Returns a zero-row batch with the original schema. Input has zero rows Returns a zero-row batch with the original schema. All rows match Retains all rows and the original schema. Processor reused for another batch Processes that batch independently; input-batch state is not retained.

FilterRows does not alter the input schema, select or rename columns, perform I/O, or coordinate pipeline execution. Cross-batch output-schema compatibility is enforced by Pipeline, not by an individual processor.

See Core Concepts for the batch model and API Reference for constructor details.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FileSystem is a protocol defining the storage-access contract used by ETLRelay's file sources and sinks.

LocalFileSystem implements this protocol by providing readable and writable binary streams for local filesystem paths.

Storage access is separated from file-format handling. LocalFileSystem does not know about CSV, Parquet, Batch, readers, writers, sources, sinks, or pipeline orchestration.

For local filesystem security, LocalFileSystem uses PathValidator to ensure that paths resolve within the configured permitted directory.

docs.title: FileSystem
docs.text:
FileSystem defines the minimal storage contract required by file sources and sinks.

It is responsible for exposing operations that open resources as binary streams:

  • open_read() opens a resource for reading.
  • open_write() opens a resource for writing.

FileSystem is not responsible for:

  • Parsing or serializing file formats.
  • Creating or interpreting Batch objects.
  • Implementing source or sink orchestration.
  • Pipeline execution.
  • Application-level logging.

The protocol is intentionally small so that multiple storage implementations can satisfy the same contract.

docs.title: LocalFileSystem
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem is responsible for:

  • Opening local files for binary reading.
  • Opening local files for binary writing.
  • Validating path containment through PathValidator.
  • Translating a FileNotFoundError raised while opening an input file into FileSystemError, including when the file disappears after path validation.
  • Returning binary streams to callers.
  • Propagating filesystem access errors.

LocalFileSystem is not responsible for:

  • Parsing CSV, Parquet, or other formats.
  • Serializing Batch objects.
  • Selecting readers or writers.
  • Creating missing parent directories.
  • Source or sink orchestration.
  • Pipeline execution.
  • Application-level logging.

The storage implementation handles filesystem existence and I/O behavior. PathValidator handles path containment.

docs.title: PathValidator
docs.text:
PathValidator determines whether a candidate path resolves within its configured base directory.

It accepts paths represented as Path objects or strings and returns the resolved path when the containment check succeeds.

It does not check whether the path exists.

This separation supports both input and output paths:

FileSource
    │
    └── Existing input path
            │
            ▼
       LocalFileSystem
            │
            ▼
         open_read()

FileSink
    │
    └── Existing or new output path
            │
            ▼
       LocalFileSystem
            │
            ▼
         open_write()

docs.title: Dependency Relationship
docs.text:
FileSource and FileSink depend on the FileSystem protocol rather than directly on LocalFileSystem.

FileSource ──┐
             ├──> FileSystem
FileSink ────┘
                  ▲
                  │ implements
                  │
             LocalFileSystem
                  │
                  ▼
             PathValidator

The current storage implementation is LocalFileSystem. S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends are not included in v0.4.0 or the planned v1.0.0 scope.

The FileSystem protocol establishes a small storage-access boundary, but it does not mean that remote backends are implemented or committed for a future release. Additional storage and platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 if concrete requirements justify them. No particular backend or release date is promised.

docs.title: FileSource
docs.text:
FileSource
    │
    ├── FileSystem.open_read(path)
    │          │
    │          ▼
    │       BinaryIO
    │          │
    │          ▼
    └────── Reader.read(stream)
                   │
                   ▼
             Iterable[Batch]

The storage component opens the resource, and the reader interprets its contents. The reader may produce multiple batches from one resource.

docs.title: FileSink
docs.text:
FileSink
    │
    ├── FileSystem.open_write(path)
    │          │
    │          ▼
    │       BinaryIO
    │          │
    │          ▼
    └────── Writer.write(batches, stream)
                   │
                   ▼
              Serialized data

The writer serializes the supplied batches into the output stream. The storage component determines where the stream is stored.

FileSource and FileSink manage the streams they open.

FileSource.read() performs file access lazily, as its returned generator is consumed. The input stream is closed when iteration completes, reading raises an exception, or the generator is explicitly closed. Consumers that stop iterating early should explicitly close the generator when deterministic cleanup is required.

FileSink closes the output stream after writing succeeds or fails. Exceptions raised by the reader or writer propagate to the caller without being converted into generic source or sink exceptions.

Opening an output uses truncating write mode. If a writer fails, a partial or empty output file may remain; an existing destination may already have been truncated. The storage contract does not guarantee rollback or atomic replacement.

docs.text:
from typing import BinaryIO

from etlrelay.security import PathValidator


class LocalFileSystem:
    def __init__(self, path_validator: PathValidator) -> None:
        self._path_validator = path_validator

    def open_read(self, path: str) -> BinaryIO:
        ...

    def open_write(self, path: str) -> BinaryIO:
        ...

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Operation Expected behavior open_read(path) Validates path containment and opens the file in binary read mode (rb). It does not perform a separate existence check before opening. open_write(path) Validates path containment and opens the file in binary write mode (wb). Open a nonexistent input file Translates FileNotFoundError from the open operation into FileSystemError. Open a new output with an existing parent directory Creates the destination file. Open an existing output Truncates its existing contents when the file is opened. Open an output whose parent directory is missing Propagates FileNotFoundError; parent directories are not created automatically. Access a path outside the permitted base Raises PathValidationError. Encounter another filesystem failure Propagates the original filesystem exception.

The behavior above describes LocalFileSystem. The FileSystem protocol defines the stream-opening interface; implementations must document and satisfy the behavioral contract expected by their consumers.

Both operations return binary streams owned by the caller. Direct callers must close returned streams. When the streams are used through FileSource or FileSink, those components manage their respective stream lifetimes.

PathValidator is responsible for path containment, not existence or access-permission checks. Filesystem operations determine whether a resource can be opened.

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem has one primary responsibility: providing local filesystem access.

Path containment is delegated to PathValidator, while parsing and serialization are delegated to readers and writers.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
Additional storage implementations can satisfy FileSystem without requiring modifications to FileSource or FileSink.

The current implementation does not require a storage factory, registry, or plugin mechanism.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text:
Any implementation satisfying FileSystem can be supplied to a file source or sink, provided it preserves the protocol's behavioral contract.

Implementations must return usable binary streams and document their storage-specific behavior consistently.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text:
FileSystem exposes only two operations:

  • Opening a resource for reading.
  • Opening a resource for writing.

It does not expose unrelated filesystem administration operations such as directory traversal, permissions management, metadata management, or deletion.

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
FileSource and FileSink depend on FileSystem, not on LocalFileSystem.

LocalFileSystem depends on PathValidator to enforce local path containment.

This keeps the higher-level components independent of local filesystem details.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The storage protocol operates on binary streams rather than requiring callers to read or write an entire resource as bytes.

This allows readers and writers to operate on streams without requiring the storage component to load the entire serialized resource into memory first.

Readers and writers operate on binary streams, so they do not need to know where the data is stored. The current implementation provides local filesystem access through LocalFileSystem. Additional implementations would require their own implementation and contract tests; none is included in the v0.4.0 milestone or planned v1.0.0 scope.

LocalFileSystem should continue using Python's standard filesystem APIs and pathlib.Path internally.

PathValidator remains responsible for local path containment. LocalFileSystem remains responsible for existence checks and filesystem operations.

No additional abstractions such as storage factories, registries, remote filesystem base classes, or generic resource managers are required at this stage.

This overview shows how the main components relate. The linked architecture pages describe each boundary in more detail.

docs.title: Component responsibilities
docs.text:
Component Responsibility Batch Wraps the Apache Arrow table used as the pipeline's common tabular representation. Source Produces an iterable of batches. Processor Transforms one batch and returns one batch through process(batch: Batch) -> Batch. Sink Consumes an iterable of processed batches. Pipeline Applies processors in order and validates the schema of processed output batches during a run. FileSource / FileSink Compose storage access with reading or writing. FileSystem Opens readable or writable binary streams. Reader / Writer Convert between a stream format and the common batch representation. LocalFileSystem, CsvReader, CsvWriter Provide the current local-filesystem and CSV implementations.

The diagram shows the current local CSV composition, not an exhaustive list of every possible implementation. The built-in processors are documented in SelectColumns and RenameColumns, FilterRows, and the API Reference.

docs.title: SQL source and sink
docs.text: SqlSource and SqlSink implement the core source/sink contracts directly. They do not pass through FileSystem, Reader, or Writer. SqlSource executes parameterized SQLAlchemy text queries and produces a batch for non-empty results; SqlSink appends rows to a pre-existing table with a separate transaction per non-empty batch. See SQL source and sink for the full behavior and limitations.

docs.title: Batch and empty-data distinction
docs.text: A Batch is a single data unit backed by an Arrow table. A zero-row table is still a batch and retains its schema. An empty source iterable contains no batches; in that case the pipeline does not invoke processors or the sink. See Pipeline for the full execution and schema-validation contract.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
PathValidator is a security component responsible for ensuring that a filesystem path resolves within an explicitly permitted base directory.

It resolves candidate paths before checking containment, preventing relative path traversal and symlink-based paths from escaping the permitted boundary.

PathValidator is intentionally small and independent of ETLRelay's storage, source, sink, reader, and writer implementations. LocalFileSystem uses it to validate local filesystem paths before performing I/O.

Path validation does not require the candidate to exist. Filesystem existence and access errors are handled by the storage component.

docs.text:
PathValidator is responsible for:

  • Accepting an optional base directory during construction.
  • Defaulting the base directory to the current working directory when none is provided.
  • Resolving the base directory and candidate paths.
  • Determining whether a resolved candidate remains within the permitted base directory.
  • Returning the resolved path when valid.
  • Raising PathValidationError when a candidate escapes the permitted boundary.

PathValidator is not responsible for:

  • Checking whether a candidate path exists.
  • Opening, reading, or writing files.
  • Creating directories.
  • Parsing CSV or other data formats.
  • Knowing about Batch.
  • Knowing about Source, Sink, or pipeline execution.
  • Performing authorization or user-level access control.
  • Logging application-level events.

docs.title: Dependency Relationship
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem

       ▼
PathValidator

LocalFileSystem depends on PathValidator to enforce local path containment before performing filesystem operations.

PathValidator does not depend on LocalFileSystem or any higher-level ETLRelay component. It uses Python's pathlib.Path for path resolution and containment checks.

FileSource and FileSink depend on the FileSystem protocol rather than on PathValidator directly. Path validation is handled by the concrete local storage implementation.

docs.text:
from pathlib import Path


class PathValidator:
    def __init__(self, base_path: Path | None = None) -> None:
        ...

    def validate(self, path: Path | str) -> Path:
        ...


class PathValidationError(Exception):
    """Raised when a filesystem path fails validation."""

docs.text: Operation Expected behavior Construct without a base path Uses the resolved current working directory Construct with an explicit base path Uses the resolved supplied directory as the permitted boundary Validate a contained relative path Returns the resolved path Validate a contained absolute path Returns the resolved path Validate the base directory itself Returns the resolved base path Validate a path containing safe . or .. segments Returns the resolved path if it remains within the boundary Validate a path containing traversal that escapes the base Raises PathValidationError Validate an absolute path outside the base Raises PathValidationError Validate a path with a similar directory-name prefix outside the base Raises PathValidationError Validate a symlink resolving inside the base Returns the resolved target path Validate a symlink resolving outside the base Raises PathValidationError Validate a nonexistent path inside the base Returns the resolved path; existence is not checked

docs.title: Single Responsibility Principle
docs.text:
PathValidator has one reason to change: the rules governing local filesystem path containment.

It does not combine path validation with filesystem I/O, data-format handling, or application logic.

docs.title: Open/Closed Principle
docs.text:
The implementation remains deliberately small. Additional path policies should be introduced only when concrete requirements justify them.

No path-policy hierarchy or configurable validation framework is required.

docs.title: Liskov Substitution Principle
docs.text: No inheritance hierarchy is required. PathValidator is a concrete security utility whose behavior is defined by its contract.

docs.title: Interface Segregation Principle
docs.text: No protocol is necessary for the current implementation. PathValidator exposes only the operation its consumer requires: validate().

docs.title: Dependency Inversion Principle
docs.text:
LocalFileSystem delegates path-containment checks to PathValidator rather than implementing its own validation logic.

PathValidator depends only on Python's standard path-handling functionality and remains independent of higher-level ETLRelay components.

docs.title: Design Constraints
docs.text:
The implementation should use pathlib.Path and explicit path containment rather than string-prefix comparisons.

The validator establishes its permitted boundary during construction:

PathValidator(base_path)
        │
        ▼
  trusted boundary
        │
        ▼
validate(candidate_path)
        │
        ├── contained ──> resolved Path
        │
        └── outside ────> PathValidationError

The containment check must occur after path resolution so that traversal segments and symlinks are evaluated against their resolved locations.

Path existence is deliberately outside this component's contract:

PathValidator
      │
      ├── contained path ──> resolved Path
      │
      └── escaping path ───> reject

LocalFileSystem
      │
      ├── open existing resource for reading
      │
      └── open destination for writing

PathValidator establishes a path-containment boundary; it is not a complete filesystem sandbox or authorization mechanism. Filesystem changes between validation and subsequent use can still create time-of-check-to-time-of-use risks.

No additional abstractions such as PathPolicy, PathResolver, or a filesystem interface are required for this component.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
FilterRows is a built-in implementation of the Processor contract. It filters a Batch using one comparison between a named column and a configured value. Comparisons and row filtering use Apache Arrow compute operations.

The processor provides a deliberately small predicate interface; it does not implement an expression language or custom casting system.

docs.title: Responsibilities and behavior
docs.text:
FilterRows stores one column name, one supported comparison operator, and one comparison value. It returns a new Batch containing rows that satisfy the predicate.

Supported operators are ==, !=, <, <=, >, and >=.

Scenario Behavior Unsupported operator Raises ValueError during initialization. Unknown or ambiguous column Raises ValueError when processing a batch. Incompatible comparison types Raises TypeError; no custom casting is performed. Comparison evaluates to null Excludes the row. No rows match Returns a zero-row batch with the original schema. Input has zero rows Returns a zero-row batch with the original schema. All rows match Retains all rows and the original schema. Processor reused for another batch Processes that batch independently; input-batch state is not retained.

FilterRows does not alter the input schema, select or rename columns, perform I/O, or coordinate pipeline execution. Cross-batch output-schema compatibility is enforced by Pipeline, not by an individual processor.

See Core Concepts for the batch model and API Reference for constructor details.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Reader and Writer define small protocols for converting between serialized data and ETLRelay's common Batch representation.

A Reader consumes a binary stream and produces an iterable of Batch objects.

A Writer consumes an iterable of Batch objects and serializes them to a binary stream.

The protocols separate format-specific parsing and serialization from storage access. Higher-level components such as FileSource and FileSink compose these protocols with a FileSystem implementation.

The concrete implementations are CsvReader, CsvWriter, ParquetReader, and ParquetWriter.

docs.title: Reader
docs.text:
Reader defines the contract for converting serialized data from a binary stream into ETLRelay batches.

It is responsible only for defining the reading operation and its return contract.

Reader is not responsible for:

  • Opening filesystem resources.
  • Selecting storage backends or resource paths.
  • Validating local filesystem path containment.
  • Writing serialized data.
  • Transforming batches as part of pipeline processing.
  • Orchestrating pipelines.

docs.title: Writer
docs.text:
Writer defines the contract for serializing ETLRelay batches to a binary stream.

It is responsible only for defining the writing operation and its input contract.

Writer is not responsible for:

  • Opening filesystem resources.
  • Selecting storage backends or destination paths.
  • Validating local filesystem path containment.
  • Reading serialized data.
  • Applying pipeline transformations.
  • Orchestrating pipelines.

docs.title: CsvReader
docs.text:
CsvReader implements Reader for CSV data.

It is responsible for:

  • Parsing CSV data from a supplied binary stream.
  • Converting parsed data into ETLRelay Batch objects.
  • Returning the resulting batches through an iterable.

It is not responsible for:

  • Opening or locating files.
  • Validating filesystem paths.
  • Writing CSV data.
  • Applying pipeline transformations.
  • Managing pipeline execution.

The underlying parsing implementation uses PyArrow.

docs.title: CsvWriter
docs.text:
CsvWriter implements Writer for CSV data.

It is responsible for:

  • Accepting an iterable of Batch objects.
  • Serializing the batches as CSV data.
  • Writing the serialized output to the supplied binary stream.

It is not responsible for:

  • Opening or locating the destination.
  • Validating filesystem paths.
  • Reading CSV data.
  • Applying pipeline transformations.
  • Managing pipeline execution.

The underlying serialization implementation uses PyArrow.

docs.title: ParquetReader
docs.text:
ParquetReader implements Reader for Parquet files. It uses PyArrow's Parquet file API to read a binary stream and yield ETLRelay Batch objects. It preserves the schema and supported Arrow types represented in the file, including null values for the supported types exercised by the tests. A zero-row Parquet file produces one zero-row batch with its schema, so an empty dataset remains distinguishable from a source that yields no batches.

The input stream must be seekable because PyArrow's Parquet API needs to access file metadata and column data through a seekable file-like object. The generic BinaryIO protocol does not express this requirement. The caller retains responsibility for opening and closing the stream. Malformed Parquet content raises pyarrow.ArrowInvalid; I/O errors may propagate as OSError.

docs.title: ParquetWriter
docs.text:
ParquetWriter implements Writer for Parquet data. It serializes all supplied batches into one Parquet file through PyArrow. The first batch establishes the output schema, and later batches must have a matching schema; ETLRelay does not merge schemas or cast incompatible batches automatically. A zero-row batch is valid because it still supplies a schema and creates a valid zero-row Parquet file.

An empty batch iterable raises WriterError: without a batch, the writer has no schema with which to initialize the Parquet file. This differs from an iterable containing one zero-row batch. The writer finalizes the Parquet container but does not take ownership of the caller's underlying stream.

docs.title: Dependency Relationship
docs.text:
FileSource ──> Reader
                  ▲
                  ├── CsvReader
                  └── ParquetReader

FileSink ───> Writer
                  ▲
                  ├── CsvWriter
                  └── ParquetWriter

FileSource depends on the Reader protocol rather than on a particular format implementation. FileSink similarly depends on the Writer protocol.

Storage access is a separate dependency:

FileSource ──> FileSystem
FileSink   ──> FileSystem

The filesystem opens the resource and supplies a binary stream. The configured reader or writer operates on that stream without selecting the storage location or inspecting a filename extension.

CSV and Parquet are supported through the existing local-file composition model. The only storage implementation included in v0.4.0 is LocalFileSystem. S3, HDFS, and other remote-storage backends are outside both v0.4.0 and the planned v1.0.0 scope.

Additional storage or platform integrations may be reviewed after v1.0.0 based on concrete requirements, without a commitment to specific backends or release dates.
